_readme: Dated events and specific figures only. Every fact needs a source_url and as_of date. This is the registry that prevents the pipeline from inventing history.

domain_01_service_design.fact: Union Pacific announced Unified Plan 2020 in September 2018, implementing Precision Scheduled Railroading (PSR) principles, with phased rollout beginning October 1, 2018 starting on the eastern North/South corridor between Wisconsin and Texas.

PSR was created/popularized by the late E. Hunter Harrison, who implemented it at Canadian National and Canadian Pacific before his final role as CEO of CSX; UP became (per trade coverage at the time) the second US-based Class I to adopt it after CSX, though as of 2022 trade coverage PSR was in place or under adoption by all Class I railroads except BNSF.

UP's own initial 'Blend and Balance' PSR design did not perform reliably in the field — by CEO Lance Fritz's own account, by mid-2018 UP determined the transportation plan as originally conceived was 'virtually impossible to execute reliably and consistently,' leading to a redesign in August 2018 that became Unified Plan 2020.

The STB sent a letter to UP CEO Lance Fritz shortly after the Unified Plan 2020 announcement, asking UP to provide updates on the operating changes — illustrating that even a non-merger service change draws STB oversight attention.

domain_02_dispatching.fact: Union Pacific's Harriman Dispatching Center opened in Omaha in 1989, centralizing 10 regional dispatching centers into one location.

domain_03_terminal_yard.fact: Bailey Yard in North Platte, Nebraska is the largest railroad classification yard in the world: approximately 2,850 acres, about 8 miles long, 315 miles of track, named for former UP President Edd H. Bailey. It has 17 receiving and 16 departure tracks, two humps (eastbound ~34 ft, westbound ~20 ft), and 114 bowl tracks (49 westbound, 65 eastbound). It handles roughly 10,000-14,000 railcars and ~139 trains every 24 hours, sorting about 3,000 cars/day at up to 4 cars/minute. UP employs more than 2,600 people in North Platte.

domain_04_crew_management.fact: PS Technology (PST) is a wholly-owned subsidiary of Union Pacific Railroad, building crew management/timekeeping software sold industry-wide.

On August 11, 2026, the Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals upheld FRA's 2024 two-person minimum crew rule in a 2-1 decision, rejecting a challenge from the Association of American Railroads, the American Short Line and Regional Railroad Association, and six railroads including Union Pacific. The court denied the petitions for review but did not vacate the rule.
The FRA received approximately 13,500 public comments on the proposed 2024 crew size rule, with more than 98.5% supporting it.

As part of the new Eagle Pass gateway process (effective Nov 20, 2025), Ferromex crews operating into the US have been 'trained and qualified by Union Pacific, including certification' — a concrete, sourced example of cross-border crew qualification process, relevant to RR-04 territory qualification content.

domain_05_mechanical.fact: UP employees are responsible for train inspections at the initial terminal and after every 1,000 miles of operation, per UP's own facilities disclosure; detecting component defects before they reach the mainline is framed as avoiding derailments that affect safety, service reliability, and customer commitments.

UP operates more than 50 locomotive and rail car facilities across its 23-state system. The Downing B. Jenks Shop in North Little Rock, Arkansas is the largest and is described as North America's foremost locomotive overhaul facility (1,000+ employees); it dismantled and rebuilt 200 locomotive units in 2023. North Platte, NE is historically UP's second-largest shop.

UP signed a $1.2 billion agreement with Wabtec to modernize its AC4400 locomotive fleet with Wabtec's Modular Control Architecture (a standardized computing/software platform), enabling condition-based maintenance via real-time fault/performance reporting instead of strictly time-based service intervals. The program targets an 80% reliability improvement and a 14% increase in tractive effort.

At UP's Proviso Locomotive Shop (Illinois), the Mechanical team identified that winter condensation in low-horsepower locomotives' air brake systems could freeze components like the A-1 charging valve; the team's fix required changing an existing locomotive shutdown operating-rule policy to allow crews to leave units running under an accepted shutdown protocol.

UP is developing a battery-electric locomotive fleet as a next step in emissions reduction, with mechanical engineering staff writing new technical specifications for it as of an October 2021 UP publication.

domain_06_engineering.fact: Union Pacific became the first Class I railroad to modernize all three core operating platforms — Positive Train Control, computer-aided dispatch, and transportation management — cutting over to NetControl on January 6, 2024, replacing the mainframe Transportation Control System (TCS) it had run for over 50 years.

In March 2020, Union Pacific petitioned FRA for a temporary suspension of 49 CFR 213.233(c) to pilot autonomous track geometry measurement systems in place of traditional inspection methods, on segments of its SPSCL and Sunset routes across 5 subdivisions.

As of an August 2024 trade profile, Union Pacific's track inspection fleet comprised one crewed traditional track geometry car, a crewed Hi-Rail system, ten automated locomotive-mounted inspection systems, and three boxcar-mounted autonomous systems; most inspection miles are completed by the locomotive- and boxcar-mounted systems.
Union Pacific reports track-caused defects down approximately 85% over the roughly five years since it began its automated track inspection program (i.e., program start approximately 2019).

Union Pacific was one of four railroads (with BNSF, Norfolk Southern, and CSX) that jointly submitted the I-ETMS PTC Development Plan v2.0 to FRA for Type Approval in June 2011, built on Wabtec's I-ETMS (formerly V-ETMS) product.

NAMING CAVEAT — do not conflate: 'ATIP' (Automated Track Inspection Program) is the FRA's own government-run track inspection car fleet, which conducts compliance surveys of 50,000-100,000 miles of track per year across the network, including on UP track. It is not documented as UP's internal program name. CN separately operates its own branded 'Autonomous Track Inspection Program,' also abbreviated ATIP, which is a different company's program.

domain_07_safety_regulatory.fact: GCOR (General Code of Operating Rules) is used by Class I railroads west of Chicago (including UP), most Class II railroads, and many short lines; railroads in the northeast US generally use NORAC instead. GCOR's 9th edition took effect September 23, 2025 per one trade summary, superseding prior editions and applying to BNSF, UP, and other adopters.
FRA 2025 data shows overall train accidents down 14% year-over-year, cited by a US DOT representative in the context of the Aug 2026 crew-size ruling as evidence of continued safety improvement.

domain_08_hazmat_environmental.fact: The AskRail app was launched in October 2014 as a joint effort of America's Class I freight railroads, Amtrak, the International Association of Fire Chiefs, AAR, and Railinc (which administers the app). It serves more than 2.3 million first responders across 49 states, the District of Columbia, and 8 Canadian provinces, available in English and French across the US, Canada, and Mexico.

TRANSCAER (Transportation Community Awareness and Emergency Response) was founded in 1986 by Union Pacific and the Dow Chemical Company as a voluntary national outreach effort helping communities prepare for and respond to hazmat transportation incidents; it is now an industry-wide program.

The rail industry's shared hazmat emergency-response training facility, SERTC, is located in Pueblo, Colorado, and trains thousands of first responders annually (one program cited a target of training 2,000 first responders in a given year).

domain_09_intermodal_automotive.fact: UP's Dallas Intermodal Terminal, a $100 million facility begun June 2004, was the first UP intermodal yard to introduce satellite-guided (GPS) crane technology allowing safer dual-crane operation on parallel tracks; it decreased truck processing time from 4 minutes to as little as 30-90 seconds and provided over 4,000 staging spaces for trailers/containers.

UP's Joliet, Illinois Intermodal Terminal is 785 acres, opened to handle international shipment growth to/from Chicago; at the time of opening it had six tracks to stage rail cars, four cranes, two rubber-tired mobile 'packers,' GPS-guided lifting, and 3,400+ staging spaces.

UP's ICTF (Intermodal Container Transfer Facility) in Long Beach, California installed the industry's first-ever hybrid electric crane to reduce emissions, and UP has upgraded lift equipment engines in California to more stringent emission levels.

UP opened (expected Q1 2024) a new international intermodal terminal in Phoenix, owned and operated by UP at its downtown Phoenix rail yard, with drayage support from Duncan & Son Lines; serves as a connection between LA Basin ports and the US Southwest.

At UP's Global IV Intermodal Terminal outside Chicago, drayman/BCO complaints about container-pull wait times were diagnosed using gate-technology data, leading UP to work with select beneficial cargo owners on optimal pull times to improve driver efficiency — a concrete, sourced example of how UPGo/gate-data feedback loops actually function operationally.

domain_10_commercial.fact: Loup Logistics launched Nov 1, 2017 as a wholly-owned Union Pacific subsidiary, formed by merging four prior UP subsidiaries: Union Pacific Distribution Services (UPDS), Streamline, ShipCarsNow, and Insight Network Logistics (INL). The name 'Loup' (pronounced 'loop') references the logistics 'loop' and keeping customers 'in the loop'; the logo uses negative space to depict a rail crossing and the letters 'UP.'

Loup's ShipmentVision platform provides 24/7 shipment track-and-trace across all rail carriers and modes, customizable dashboards, dynamic ETAs and transit-time calculators — available only to Loup customers.
Loup's transload service bundles rail, transloading, and truck delivery under an all-inclusive 'One Plus' price, available by carload, truckload, or by weight.

domain_11_interline_equipment.fact: Umler (Universal Machine Language Equipment Register) was established in 1968, originally using punch cards then magnetic tapes, moving to EDI/ANSI X12 standards in the 1980s. It is managed by Railinc for the AAR and registers over 2 million pieces of North American rail equipment with less than 1% error rate.

On November 20, 2025, Union Pacific changed its interchange process with Ferromex (FXE) at the Eagle Pass, Texas gateway, moving the crew/train transfer point from the International Railway Bridge itself to UP's Clark Park Yard, 7 rail miles from the border. Mexican Ferromex crews (trained and certified by UP) now bring trains to the yard before a US crew takes over, reducing bridge transit time by roughly 50% and implemented as part of US Customs and Border Protection's Secure Corridor Initiative.

Eagle Pass-Piedras Negras is UP's (and BNSF's, as a trackage-rights tenant) #2 US-Mexico rail gateway by volume; the #1 gateway, Laredo-Nuevo Laredo, is controlled by CPKC (Canadian Pacific Kansas City), not UP. In an October data point cited in 2025 trade coverage, UP/BNSF interchanged an average of 16 trains/day with Ferromex via Eagle Pass, versus CPKC's ~24 trains/day at Laredo.

In September 2023, US Customs and Border Protection closed the Eagle Pass and El Paso rail border crossings due to a migrant crisis, halting UP and BNSF interchange with Ferromex for several days; UP donated $100,000 to the Eagle Pass mayor's discretionary fund during the closure and staged en-route trains to manage congestion. A similar closure recurred in December 2023.

UP states its Mexico gateway coverage is the broadest and most direct of any US Class I railroad, connecting with Mexican railroads FXE (Ferromex) and KCSM (now part of CPKC de Mexico); named gateways for at least LPG/petroleum shipments include Calexico, El Paso, Nogales, Eagle Pass, Laredo, and Brownsville.

domain_12_technology.fact: PRIMARY SOURCE (UP FY2025 10-K): UP describes 'Physics Train Builder,' proprietary technology evaluating train and route characteristics to enable proactive derailment-prevention intervention by its 'Operating Practices Command Center.' The same filing states UP's autonomous geometry car fleet inspects 500,000 miles of track annually, and that this technology and data have helped significantly reduce track-caused derailments over the last 10 years.

PRIMARY SOURCE (UP FY2025 10-K): UP runs 'COMMIT' (Situational Awareness Testing), a program that observes, tests, and coaches employees on work-rule compliance with emphasis on in-the-field training rather than traditional classroom learning, plus a 'Peer-to-Peer Engagement' program driving employee ownership of safety programs.

As of a 2018 interview, then-CIO Lynden Tennison described UP's active pursuit of Big Data, predictive/video analytics, machine and deep learning, AI, and autonomous vehicles; UP had deployed some Machine Vision portals and stated a theoretical network-wide maximum of ~70 if deployed on all high-traffic mainlines, with no expansion plans at that time. Current CIO (2024-2026 sourcing) is Rahul Jalali, who has described UP's strategy as transforming it into a 'platform company' modeled on Apple/Google/Amazon-style integration, with a 'secure-by-design' cybersecurity approach and named future directions including generative AI and zero-trust cybersecurity.

domain_13_finance.fact: UP's own risk disclosure states fuel surcharge programs trail fluctuations in fuel price by approximately two months, which the company identifies as a significant source of quarter-over-quarter and year-over-year revenue volatility, particularly during rapid price changes.
domain_13_finance.as_of: 2015 (mechanism description; UP's 10-K risk-factor language on this point is stable across years)

domain_13_finance.fact: In 2007, 20+ rail shippers (growing to 30 total complaints) filed antitrust lawsuits alleging Union Pacific and other Class I railroads engaged in price-fixing by establishing common fuel surcharges; the first suit was filed in US District Court in New Jersey on May 14, 2007. UPRR and three other Class I railroads remained named defendants per UP's own 10-K disclosure. This is a real, citable historical pain point for fuel-surcharge process design — not an invented one.
domain_13_finance.as_of: 2007-2015 (disclosed across multiple 10-Ks; verify current litigation status before citing as ongoing)

domain_13_finance.fact: The STB issued a decision limiting how US railroads calculate fuel surcharges on STB-regulated traffic (referenced in UP's FY2006 10-K); UP stated at the time it did not believe the decision would prevent it from using fuel surcharges on most or all of its traffic.
domain_13_finance.as_of: 2006-2007 (verify current STB fuel-surcharge rule status before citing as UP's present practice)

domain_13_finance.fact: CAUTION — commodity group count has changed over time: UP's FY2006/2007/2008 10-Ks describe 'six commodity groups.' By the 2022 and 2023 10-Q filings, UP describes 'three commodity groups.' Verify UP's current commodity-group structure directly before writing any RR-13 or RR-10 process that names a specific count or lists the groups by name — do not assume either the six-group or three-group structure without checking the most recent 10-K.
domain_13_finance.as_of: 2023-Q3 vs 2007-2008 (structure has changed; re-verify before use)

domain_14_hr_labor.fact: UP's TE&Y (Train, Engine & Yard) New Hire Training program is an 8-week 'sandbox' program using real equipment (locomotives, rail cars, track, switches) under instructor supervision, with learners spending ~85% of time in the field. It replaced an older process that took 18 weeks and emphasized classroom theory over hands-on training; the redesign was driven by feedback requesting more hands-on car-handling training. Recognized as a Training Top 100 Best Practice (Training magazine).

As of June 2012, UP built a fleet of 5 mobile classroom trailers to bring operations/safety training and locomotive simulators to engineer and conductor locations across its 23-state system. Each trailer has 7 workstations (2 employees each); doors can be opened by employee ID entry or remotely by instructors based in Salt Lake City, Utah and Omaha, Nebraska, who can also assist trainees via webcam.

In 2022, UP averaged nearly 47 hours of training per employee, a 62% year-over-year increase attributed to robust hiring; team members completed approximately 10,000 skill-enhancement courses that year across topics including CPR, welding, ballast tamping, track inspection, and locomotive maintenance.

CROSS-REFERENCE TO PILOT PROCESS RR-03-05-01: UP's own training materials describe the hands-on portion of new-hire air brake training in specific procedural detail — after verifying 75 psi on the rear of the train with a handheld gauge or End-of-Train device, the engineer makes a 20-pound reduction, and students then conduct a safety inspection while rechecking a 100% set of the brakes, per a Class 1 Initial Terminal Air Brake Test. This is real, sourced procedural detail that could strengthen RR-03-05-01's description if you choose to regenerate it with a richer domain_03 registry.

domain_15_merger_integration.fact: Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern filed their first STB major merger application in December 2025; the STB rejected it as incomplete in a unanimous decision on January 16, 2026, citing inconsistencies in market share projections. The companies filed a revised application on April 30, 2026.

On May 28, 2026, the STB unanimously accepted the revised UP/NS merger application as complete, but held the proceedings (including environmental review) in abeyance and ordered the companies to submit supplemental information by July 27, 2026. The STB will hold at least 12 in-person public meetings plus virtual meetings as part of the EIS process.

UP and NS completed their supplemental information responses to the STB in a filing around July 27, 2026, and offered additional voluntary customer protection commitments (service protections, fixed pricing agreements) beyond those in prior rail mergers.

The STB resumed its review of the UP/NS merger in mid-August 2026 (having paused it in late May 2026), adopting a procedural schedule with a projected timeline running through at least May 28, 2027. The STB explicitly stated resumption does not mean approval. The STB denied UP/NS's request for expedited/separate review of the proposed divestiture of control of the Terminal Railroad Association of St. Louis, and directed the companies to re-submit data omitted during refiling by August 28, 2026.

The deal is valued at approximately $85 billion and is described by the companies as creating the first modern coast-to-coast ("transcontinental") US freight rail network, uniting two of the six remaining Class I railroads. UP CEO is Jim Vena; NS President and CEO is Mark George.

The merger application projects $133 million in annual capital synergies from leveraging the combined network and fleet more efficiently. Both companies describe a recent history of managing large, complex system changes as evidence for a 'precision integration' approach.

Shipper groups (e.g., cited spokesperson O'Liddy) have formally urged the STB to reject the merger, arguing it would cause 'grave competitive impacts that cannot be effectively remedied through the STB's conditioning authority,' particularly for captive shippers. As of the most recent sourcing, the merger remains pending before the STB and has not been approved.
